Estimating the replicability of psychology experiments after an initial failure to replicate

2026-11-19 · Metacheck 0.4.4.25

To fix (6)

To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

For instance, the rescue of Paxton et al. (2012) switched from using the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT) which many online participants are over-familiar with to using the newer CRT-2, which is used less but attempts to measure the same construct (Thomson & Oppenheimer, 2016).

With one exception, samples were collected on Prolific (the rescue of Yeshurun & Levy, 2003 ran in person on the Stanford student subject pool).

Across the 16 Prolific studies, we spent $5471, for an average of $342 per project.

However, rescue projects varied in how close the re-replications actually were, often due to limitations in the availability of original stimuli and original instructions, in addition to the use of primarily online subject pools.

The first replication struggled to recruit participants who were naive to the problem (an exclusion criterion), and many participants gave very short text responses in the provided text box (only textual responses were allowed).

The rescue targeted these issues by adding a pre-screening that ensured participants were not familiar with the Monty Hall problem, changed the content items for the problem and changed its name (to reduce googling for answers), and had participants upload drawings for their justifications.

It is reasonable to expect online studies of reading time to be noisier than in-person studies because the environments participants completed the study in vary much more online.

Students were enrolled in a highly competitive graduate program where it is expected that PhD students author peer-reviewed papers.

find a significant difference between conditions, and the rescuer speculated that this was due to a smaller sample size and a skew toward liberal political beliefs in the participant pool.

The rescuer removed the sub-condition and used questions from the CRT-2, out of concern that Prolific participants would be familiar with the original CRT questions.

The rescue was also conducted online, but the rescuer made a series of user interface changes, a comprehension check, and exclusion criteria to ensure that participants understood the instructions, found the task convenient to interact with, and were engaged throughout the experiment.

When we reached out to the original authors, they offered to run a parallel rescue on their student subject pool, which we have here as an additional replication.

Participants were asked to recall experiences where they had either a low or high amount of control and then to report their level of physical pain.

To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 2 potential power analyses.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8’ to check the contents of 2 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: statistical_test, sample_size, alpha_level, power, effect_size, effect_size_metric, software

power_id power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
1 apriori NA 12 NA 0.8 NA other NA
2 apriori NA NA NA NA NA NA NA
power_id text
1;2 The rescue of Krauss & Wang (2003) was successful despite an unsuccessful replication. This study looked at the influence of guided thinking on whether people gave correct justifications (drawn or written) for their answer on the Monty Hall problem. The original paper reported correct justifications from 2/67 (3%) participants in the control condition and 13/34 (38%) in the guided thinking condition. The first replication struggled to recruit participants who were naive to the problem (an exclusion criterion), and many participants gave very short text responses in the provided text box (only textual responses were allowed). The replication found 0/8 correct justifications in the control and 0/11 in the guided thinking condition. While we cannot know for sure what caused the non-replication, there were clear problems observable from the small final sample and low-quality responses. The rescue targeted these issues by adding a pre-screening that ensured participants were not familiar with the Monty Hall problem, changed the content items for the problem and changed its name (to reduce googling for answers), and had participants upload drawings for their justifications. We believe these changes collectively brought the rescue closer to the intent of the original. The rescue had 1/40 (2.5%) correct justifications in the control condition and 6/35 (17%) in the guided thinking condition. This effect was significant, though smaller than the effect in the original. Ngo et al. (2019) was a second successful rescue. The original study found a large effect; hence the first replication, powering for 80% power on the reported effect, recruited a small sample of 12 people. This small study failed to find the original effect (now known to be due to a coding error). The rescue, powered using 2.5x the original sample (as recommended by Simonsohn, 2015), recovered a clear effect (albeit a much smaller one) with the same coding error. After correcting the coding error, both the first replication and the rescue have effects that are only somewhat smaller than the original. An additional replication from the literature, Ngo & Newcombe (2021) successfully replicated Ngo et al. (2019). There are reasons to think that some effect sizes in the literature may be inflated (Camerer et al., 2018; Open Science Collaboration, 2015), and it is also possible that changes to experiments or moving data collection online could result in noisier samples and thus smaller effect sizes. Therefore, replications with smaller samples than the original (even if powered to the original effect size), may not be very diagnostic, and could potentially benefit from a re-replication.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Marginal Significance

What we found

You described 1 effect with terms related to ‘marginally significant’.

Show details

You described effects with terms related to ‘marginally significant’. If p values above 0.05 are interpreted as an effect, you inflate the alpha level, and increase the Type 1 error rate. If a p value is higher than the prespecified alpha level, it should be interpreted as a non-significant result.

Text Section Header
None of the pre-registered correlates meet the conventional significance threshold; the two correlates based on ratios that reflect a relatively smaller replication sample size are marginally significant. Original study First replication Rescue Additional replication

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate at which non-significant p-values are interpreted as marginally significant, see:

Olsson-Collentine A, van Assen MALM, Hartgerink CHJ (2019). “The Prevalence of Marginally Significant Results in Psychology Over Time.” Psychological Science, 30, 576–586. doi:10.1177/0956797619830326.

For the list of terms used to identifify marginally significant results, see this blog post by Matthew Hankins.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 4 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p<.05 Scientists’ intuitions about whether a replication is successful and whether an effect provides support for a hypothesis (including heuristic cutoffs like p<.05) do not always align with measures of statistical consistency (Patil et al., 2016).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (5)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .953 Corrected: r = .015, p = .953 (published: r = .027, p = .919).
p = .919 Corrected: r = .015, p = .953 (published: r = .027, p = .919).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the manuscript names a study (ex12) with no matching files in the repository; the repository separates out studies (ex1, ex5, ex3, ex2) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 3 naming problems that should be fixed, and 355 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 1 code file.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 1 code file.

File name install.packages() calls found
1159352_e9a668d9124f415e8831bab302f49b6b.R install.packages(“metafor”)

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 12 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 87 distinct packages/libraries: apaTables, BayesFactor, bookdown, boot, brms, broom, broom.mixed, car, cowplot, csv, data.table, dplyr, DT, effectsize, effsize, emmeans, esc, ez, forcats, foreign, ggplot2, ggpubr, ggrepel, ggstance, ggthemes, glmnet, googledrive, grid, gridExtra, haven, here, Hmisc, imager, interactions, irr, jsonlite, kableExtra, knitr, lattice, lintr, lme4, lmerTest, lsmeans, lsr, MASS, matrixStats, MBESS, metafor, multcomp, nnet, optimx, osfr, pander, papaja, parallel, patchwork, plotrix, plyr, png, psych, psycho, pwr, qualtRics, R.matlab, RColorBrewer, RCurl, readr, readxl, reghelper, Replicate, reshape2, rstan, rstatix, rticles, scales, sessioninfo, sjPlot, sjstats, stargazer, stringr, styler, testthat, tidybayes, tidyr, tidyverse, umx, viridis. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

To check Data Check

What we found

  • We classified 880 files: 86 data, 422 code, 365 documentation, 6 materials, 1 unknown.
  • We found 7 tabular data files and extracted 252 columns from 7 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 4 study groups (ex1, ex2, ex3, ex5), plus 1 collection-level file (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 1 trial-level data file (E-Prime / Inquisit / jsPsych / Behaverse) was recognised. These are per-participant records of a behavioural task, so they are not listed as separate datasets. Nothing is deleted. We ran automated data-quality checks on 252 columns; 7 columns have at least one potential issue (2 columns with numeric values stored as text; 2 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 1 column with inconsistent category casing; 1 column of free text that may contain personal detail; 1 column with leading/trailing whitespace). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender, Race.
Show details

This module classifies repository files and, for tabular data files available locally, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 252 columns across 7 data files.

Issues Identified

7 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 7 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

To check Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 44 R code files for reproducibility and ran 42 of them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 4 of 42 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 38 could not be checked automatically.
  • 1 referenced input unavailable (0 withheld due to size).
  • 80 installable dependencies detected.
  • 253 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 7 reported tests matched (0%).

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script needs a setting from your computer that the deposit does not hold, such as a personal key or the place of data.

  • 839090_f4ceff74ea6241969e4f35ef038ee417.R: “! Qualtrics API key and/or base URL need registering: ℹ Use `qualtrics_api_credentials()`”

We could not check these scripts. Say in the README what each setting is and how readers get it. For an online service, also save the data the script downloads, add it to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copy, as services change or close. For data that cannot be shared, say where and how readers can apply for it.

A script’s code was taken from a knitted report, as its source is not in the deposit.

A knitted report (.html) shows only the code chunks it was set to show, so code is missing from it, and we could not check the analysis. Add the R Markdown or Quarto file the report was knitted from to the deposit.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • 1102828_fa75212e4666443aa54e31e7958f4d35.R
  • hopkins_es.Rmd

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Other problems in the files

  • 344993_059f8020658d46c58beabb93b71d8959.R calls setwd(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 42 scripts: 4 ran without error, 33 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 5 scripts need the internet, which is off during the run: 1102828_fa75212e4666443aa54e31e7958f4d35.R, hopkins_es.Rmd, initial_criteria.R, manuscript_anon.Rmd, manuscript.Rmd. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this.

setwd() in the code

1 script calls setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Calls that install packages in the code

8 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

> do_rma <- function(df) {

>   return(tibble(rma_d_est = NA, rma_d_se = NA))

> do_d_predInt_het <- function(df) {
>   if (!is.na(df$d) & !is.na(df$d_se) & !is.na(df$rep_d) & !is.na(df$rep_d_se)) {
>     yio <- df$d
>     vio <- df$d_se**2
>     yir <- df$rep_d
>     vir <- df$rep_d_se**2
>     t2 <- .21**2
>     pooled.SE <- sqrt(vio + vir + t2)
>     PILo.sens <- yio - qnorm(0.975) * pooled.SE
>     PIHi.sens <- yio + qnorm(0.975) * pooled.SE
>     PIinside.sens <- (yir > PILo.sens) & (yir < PIHi.sens)

data_collection_started No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
research_questions PSYCH 251 is a graduate-level experimental methods class. In previous years, students have done replication projects which were recently analyzed for how often the replication succeeded and properties of study and replication (at https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/dpyn6/).

This year we are asking how often it is possible to “rescue” a previously failed replication by re-replicating it after modifications to address possible reasons for replication failure (https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_hyYIIEbD--fywqJwFW_3jBgj50mxm0NxiYKTPo5o4w/edit was given to students as ideas about potential sources of replication failure and corresponding modifications).

We do not make specific predictions about what fraction of re-replications will replicate the original results. We will interpret this rate as providing evidence on how initial non-replications by students should be interpreted – do they indicate that it’s worth trying again, or is the first replication failure indicative that the research is unlikely to replicate for a student?
design_dependent_variables The key dependent variable is whether the rescue (re-replication) succeeds in replicating the original result.

This will be measured by:
* (primary measure) Subjective rating of replication success on a 0-1 scale by two independent raters on the instructional team, with reconciliation via discussion between raters.
* Comparing the rescue, replication, and original on the key measure of interest (see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/dpyn6/ for extensive discussion of how key measures of interest were determined).
* Students will also rate replication success for pedagogical purposes but we will treat this as a secondary measure for exploratory analysis.

As potential covariates, we will also measure:
* The closeness of the replication (using the framework of LeBel et al 2018, Figure 1, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/2515245918787489)
* The predictors used in https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/dpyn6/ for exploratory analyses
study_design_overview This is an observational study of whether students can re-replicate results that have previously failed, so there is only 1 condition and no random assignment.

Students had the option to do rescue projects for their class project (but could also do replications instead).

The criteria for inclusion in the list of rescue options:
* Was included in the sample in https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/dpyn6/
* Had a subjective replication score of 0, .25 or .5
* The replication had a github repository available (was done in AY 2015-2016 or more recently)
* The original study had a sample size of 200 or fewer participants (for feasibility reasons if samples were increased in the rescue to increase power)
* The author of the first replication gave permission for us to re-replicate and share their work with new students
statistical_tests We will report the distribution of subjective replication success in our rescue sample

If there is a mixture of projects that succeed and fail to replicate the original results, we will qualitatively describe differences that may have played a role.


For several of these studies, we are aware of additional close replications that have taken place since the original paper was published (usually since the first class replication). We will do forward literature searches to identify other replications, so that we can compare those effect sizes as well.

* We will compare the original, 1st replication, and re-replication effect sizes, as well as any effect sizes coming from independent replications (where effect size can be computed)
* We will use p-original to evaluate how consistent the original effect size is with the totality of replications. We expect there to be a small number of replications, so we will impute the heterogeneity value as in https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/dpyn6/.
* As secondary analyses, we will calculate
a) p-original between just the original and rescue,
b) p-original between the original and all replications except the rescue (in the case where no replications are found in the literature, this is the same as done in https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/dpyn6/)
c) p-original between the rescue and all other replications.
* We will visualize the consistency between original, 1st replication, rescue, and any other replications by plotting effect size and prediction interval for each.
outliers_and_exclusions We will include all rescue projects that finish their data collection and write-up.

In the case that a project has errors that make the results uninterpretable with respect to the key hypothesis (e.g., major programming errors in the experiment), then we will withdraw the paper from the sample based on consensus between the instructor team and the student.
sample_size The sample size is determined by how many students choose to participate in the rescue project.

Any student who wishes to withdraw may do so at any point, but we will ask students to confirm their desire to participate prior to final data collection.

We will report the number of students (if any) who withdraw after data collection.
additional_comments The sample sizes for the “rescues” was pre-registered for each project and was determined on a case-by-case basis, with a general goal of collecting 2.5x the original sample size except when impractical based on budget constraints. Observational study of a set of class projects
